title: SBAR call about a patient who is getting worse
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Original practical exercise with fictional people; never imported, published or shown to learners.
gaps: No published exercise may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The wording, answers and explanations are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical or educational review.
The exercise has not been tested with learners, and its Arabic version has not been written.
The AHRQ page was only partly read: it is used for the four-part structure and nothing else.
permissions: Cited sources are paraphrased only; see the licensing register for each source's reproduction status.
objectives: Give a structured call about a deteriorating patient.
Keep the background to what the listener needs.
required_sources: Unit or national guidance on calling for review and the local escalation route
A source on SBAR use at nursing level in critical care
setup: A fictional adult, Mr A, two days after abdominal surgery, now in a fictional ICU bed; the bedside nurse phones the on-call doctor because the patient's condition is changing. This communication exercise assumes immediate bedside assessment and emergency escalation are already being arranged; it is not a reason to wait for a routine callback.

items.text: I am calling about Mr A in bed 4. Over the last hour his breathing has become faster and he is more drowsy.
items.why: It states what is happening now.

items.text: He is two days after abdominal surgery and was started on treatment for a chest infection yesterday.
items.why: It is the history the doctor needs to interpret the change.

items.text: I think he is getting worse, and I am worried about his breathing.
items.why: It is the nurse's own assessment and level of concern.

items.text: I need urgent bedside assessment now. We are activating the emergency response and continuing authorised supportive care; please confirm your response and any further instructions.
items.why: The request makes urgency and the response explicit; the nurse does not wait passively when the patient is unstable.

items.text: The ward was short-staffed last night.
items.why: Staffing concerns may need separate safety reporting; unless directly relevant to the immediate response, focus this urgent communication on the patient's current needs.

items.text: His oxygen saturation has been trending down over the last hour despite his usual oxygen therapy, and he looks more work-of-breathing to me.
items.why: It is the nurse's own clinical impression of a trend, not just a single reading, which is the kind of assessment detail a doctor needs to judge urgency.

items.text: His family visited this morning and asked when he might go home.
items.why: It is true but does not help the doctor decide what to do about the current deterioration.
